paragraphs.heading: A problem well defined
paragraphs.edited: My father has taught me many valuable life lessons. One lesson in particular, which came from his father, my grandfather, is that a problem well defined is half solved. In other words, if we can clearly define the nature of a problem, we're halfway toward finding a viable solution. Undoubtedly, the problem of evil is one of the greatest challenges raised against the Christian faith, or really against any belief system. But before we ask why God might allow evil, or how the Christian faith makes sense of evil, let's first make sure we clearly define evil.

paragraphs.heading: Not two equal forces
paragraphs.edited: Not too long ago I was in getting my hair cut, and I overheard a conversation next to me that quickly caught my attention, because the conversation was about the problem of suffering and evil. A lady said this. She said, "I think evil and good are equal but opposing forces." I had to jump in as soon as I heard this, because it seems to me that she gave a faulty view of the nature of evil. You see, good and evil are not two equal opposing forces. Rather, evil is a corruption of good. You can have good without evil, but you cannot have evil unless you first have a standard of good that can be corrupted.

paragraphs.edited: Consider an example from C.S. Lewis, a former atheist, by the way, that he wrote in his classic book Mere Christianity. "My argument against God was that the universe seemed so cruel and unjust. But how had I got this idea of just and unjust? A man does not call a line crooked unless he has some idea of a straight line. What was I comparing this universe with when I called it unjust?" As Lewis noted, justice and injustice are not equal and opposite forces. Injustice is parasitic upon a standard of justice. You cannot call a line crooked unless you first have a standard of a straight line.

paragraphs.edited: Consider another example. Let's take truth and lies. Truth is when a belief matches up with reality. In a sense, truth is telling it like it is. A lie is when you tell something that intentionally doesn't match up with reality. It's intentionally saying something that doesn't tell it like it is. You see, you can have truth in which no one tells a lie, but you cannot tell a lie unless there's first truth. Lies are a corruption of truth.

paragraphs.heading: Evil in a broken world
paragraphs.edited: This idea that evil is a corruption of good is evident in the broken world around us. Divorce is a broken marriage. Racism results from broken relationships, where we fail to recognize diversity. And addiction results from taking something meant for good, food, technology, medicine, sex, and corrupting it for something bad. Simply put, evil is when things are not the way they're supposed to be, or they are the way they're not supposed to be.

paragraphs.heading: Atheism has to borrow
paragraphs.edited: But atheism cannot account for design, or purpose, or the claim that the world is supposed to be a certain way. The reason is that on atheism the world just is. It popped into existence from nothing, and through time and chance and the laws of physics the world just arranged itself in the way we see it today. So ironically, if atheists complain about the problem of evil, they have to assume the theistic worldview to do so.

paragraphs.heading: One good reason to believe
paragraphs.edited: It's an illusion. Properly understood, the existence of evil is one good reason to believe there's a standard of good, and if there's a standard of good, the best explanation is that there's a God. Now, this doesn't explain why God allows evil. We'll get to that. But at this point it's critical to realize that when we properly define and understand the nature of evil, it's one good reason to believe that God actually exists.
